Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Keep the supplied language.", "input": "For our monthly community film night, the work begins well before anyone arrives at the old library hall. I usually start on Wednesday by checking the calendar, the room booking, and the film’s public screening terms. We choose a title that suits the season and the audience, then confirm the running time, language, and whether subtitles are available. Last October, we picked a quiet documentary about neighborhood gardens. It ran for eighty-four minutes, which left enough time for a short conversation and still let people catch the last bus home. I keep the selection details in a shared folder, along with the distributor’s contact information and a note about any screening fee. If a title needs permission, I ask early rather than assuming that a streaming subscription covers a public event.

On Thursday, I walk through the hall with the caretaker. We check that the projector, screen, speakers, and two extension leads are there, and we test the connection with the same laptop we will use on the night. The screen is on a low platform, so we put a strip of bright tape along its edge to make the step visible. I also check the lamps near the entrance and leave the aisle lights on during the film. We set out about thirty-five chairs in loose rows, with a wider gap near the back for wheelchairs and people who prefer not to sit close to the screen. There are six folding chairs in the storage cupboard if we need extra seats, but I do not block the fire exit to fit them in. A small table by the door holds the sign-in sheet, the printed schedule, and a jar for optional donations.

1. On the day, arrive about ninety minutes before the doors open. Unlock the side entrance, turn on the hall lights, and put the direction signs at the front gate and the library path. The signs should say “Film night, this way” and include the start time, not just an arrow. Bring the box of supplies from the cupboard: masking tape, marker pens, spare batteries, a phone charger, paper cups, and the first-aid kit. Check the room temperature before arranging the refreshments. We offer tea, coffee, water, and biscuits, with the ingredients written beside each plate. We do not serve food in the hall itself if the caretaker has asked us to keep the carpet clean, so the drinks stay on the tiled landing.

Next, run the film from beginning to end, including the opening titles and credits. This catches problems that a quick test may miss, such as subtitles appearing too low or a quiet section being hard to hear from the back row. Put the laptop on a stable table, keep its power cable taped down, and turn off notifications. I carry a downloaded copy only when the screening terms allow it; otherwise, we use the supplied disc or the approved playback link. Write down the exact steps for starting the film, including which input to select on the projector. Keep the remote beside the laptop rather than on the refreshments table, where it can disappear under a stack of napkins.

When guests arrive, one volunteer welcomes people and points out the accessible seating, toilets, and refreshments. Another volunteer stays near the equipment but does not stand in front of the screen. The sign-in sheet asks for a first name only, and we explain that it is for an approximate head count. If someone asks whether the event is suitable for children, answer from the film’s published guidance and be clear if we do not know. Five minutes before the start, I give a brief welcome, mention the running time, and explain that people may step out quietly at any point. I do not summarize the ending. If the film includes a difficult subject, I give a concise content note based on the distributor’s description.

During the screening, keep the entrance clear and make sure the aisle lights stay on. If the picture drops, pause the playback, check the connection, and tell the audience what is happening in a calm voice. Do not keep pressing buttons at random; use the written setup steps or ask the equipment volunteer. Afterward, leave a few minutes for people to stretch before inviting anyone who wants to stay for a discussion. We use open questions such as “What stayed with you?” rather than asking people to defend their opinions. No one has to speak, and the conversation ends at the announced time so the caretaker can lock up on schedule.

Before leaving, count the chairs, collect cups, and put the equipment back in its labeled cases. Check under the seats for lost property, wipe the refreshments table, and take rubbish to the bins outside. The volunteer on the door records the approximate attendance and any practical issue, such as a subtitle fault or a sign that was hard to see. We do not record people’s comments without asking them. Finally, switch off the projector and hall lights, check both exits, and return the key as agreed. The next morning, I send the caretaker a short thank-you and add any useful changes to the shared checklist, so the next film night starts with a clear plan rather than a search for the remote.", "output": "For our monthly community film night, the work begins well before anyone arrives at the old library hall.
